cse-1997-b-69.approach: Enumerate the only call chains the program allows. C makes no calls, so a chain through C stops at 4 records; the only way to have 5 records is Main → A → B → A → B. Then set each static link by lexical nesting and each dynamic link to the caller.

steps.title: Possible call chains
steps.body:
Calls that exist: Main→A, A→B, B→C, B→A. C calls nothing.

- Main, A, B, C — only **4** records, and C cannot extend it.
- Main, A, B, A, B — **5** records.

So the stack (bottom → top) is **Main, A, B, A, B**; the top is the second activation of B.

steps.title: Main calls A, A calls B
steps.body: Push A (local $Y$) and then B (local $Z$). A is nested directly in Main, so A's static link → Main; B is nested in A, so B's static link → the A that called it.

steps.title: B calls A, A calls B
steps.body: B calls A (recursion through B). A is declared in Main, so the new A's static link → **Main**, while its dynamic link → **B₁** (the caller). A₂ then calls B: B₂'s static and dynamic links both → **A₂**.

scene.caption: Five records: Main, A, B, A, B

steps.title: Run-time stack
steps.body:
| Record (bottom → top) | Locals | Static link | Dynamic link |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main | X | — | — |
| A₁ | Y | Main | Main |
| B₁ | Z | A₁ | A₁ |
| A₂ | Y | Main | B₁ |
| B₂ (**top**) | Z | A₂ | A₂ |

C's own $Z$ never appears because C is not active.

answer.value: Bottom→top: Main(X); A(Y) [SL→Main, DL→Main]; B(Z) [SL→A₁, DL→A₁]; A(Y) [SL→Main, DL→B₁]; B(Z) [SL→A₂, DL→A₂] = top.

pitfalls: Setting A₂'s static link to B₁ — static links follow declaration nesting, not the caller.
Including C: a chain through C has only 4 records and C calls nothing.
cse-1997-b-69.verification: Checked every chain: through C the depth is capped at 4, so Main-A-B-A-B is the unique 5-record stack.

cse-1997-b-70-a.approach: Mealy-machine minimisation by partition refinement: start with blocks of equal output pairs (P₁), then repeatedly split blocks whose members go to different blocks on some input, until nothing changes.

steps.title: Split by outputs
steps.body:
Output pairs (input 0, input 1): A, B, E, F, G give $(1,1)$; C, D, H give $(0,1)$.

$P_1=\{A,B,E,F,G\},\ \{C,D,H\}$

steps.title: Refine to P₃
steps.body:
Under $P_2$:

- A: B → AB, H → CDH; B: F → EFG, D → CDH ⇒ A, B split.
- E, F, G all go to (CDH, CDH) ⇒ stay.
- C: D → CDH, E → EFG; D: C → CDH, F → EFG; H: C → CDH, A → AB ⇒ H splits off.

$P_3=\{A\},\{B\},\{C,D\},\{E,F,G\},\{H\}$

steps.title: Check stability
steps.body:
Under $P_3$: C → (D, E) = (CD, EFG), D → (C, F) = (CD, EFG) — same. E → (D, C), F → (C, C), G → (C, D) all = (CD, CD) — same. No block splits, so $P_4=P_3$ is the equivalence partition:

$$\{A\},\ \{B\},\ \{C,D\},\ \{E,F,G\},\ \{H\}$$

pitfalls: Stopping after the output split — A and B have the same outputs but are not equivalent.
Merging H with C, D: H goes to A on input 1, which is in a different block.
cse-1997-b-70-a.verification: One more refinement pass under the final partition produced no split.

cse-1997-b-70-b.approach: Use the equivalence classes from (a) — {A}, {B}, {CD}, {EFG}, {H} — as the new states; for each class take any member's row and replace every next state by its class.

steps.title: Classes from (a)
steps.body: Equivalent classes: $A$, $B$, $CD$, $EFG$, $H$. Class map: C, D → CD; E, F, G → EFG.

steps.title: Minimal machine
steps.body:
| Present state | input = 0 | input = 1 |
|---|---|---|
| A | B, 1 | H, 1 |
| B | EFG, 1 | CD, 1 |
| CD | CD, 0 | EFG, 1 |
| EFG | CD, 1 | CD, 1 |
| H | CD, 0 | A, 1 |

5 states instead of 8.

pitfalls: Forgetting to rename next states (e.g. leaving B → F instead of B → EFG).
cse-1997-b-70-b.verification: Each member of a class gives the same renamed row: C → (CD/0, EFG/1) and D → (CD/0, EFG/1); E, F, G → (CD/1, CD/1). Partition from (a) is stable, so the 5-state machine is minimal.

cse-1997-b-71-a.approach: Pair the clauses with the distributive law $(a+b)(a+c)=a+bc$: the $w$-clauses and the $x$-clauses each collapse, and the middle clause is then absorbed.

steps.title: Collapse clause pairs
steps.body:
$(\overline{w}+y)(\overline{w}+z)=\overline{w}+yz$ and $(\overline{x}+y)(\overline{x}+z)=\overline{x}+yz$.

So $f=(\overline{w}+yz)(\overline{x}+yz)(w+\overline{x}+z)=(\overline{w}\,\overline{x}+yz)(w+\overline{x}+z)$.

steps.title: Absorb the last clause
steps.body:
$\overline{w}\,\overline{x}\cdot(w+\overline{x}+z)=\overline{w}\,\overline{x}$ (contains $\overline{x}$) and $yz\cdot(w+\overline{x}+z)=yz$ (contains $z$).

$$f=\overline{w}\,\overline{x}+yz$$

steps.title: Minimality
steps.body: On the K-map the 1s are $m_0,m_1,m_2,m_3,m_7,m_{11},m_{15}$. Both quads are essential prime implicants and together cover all 7 ones, so $f=\overline{w}\,\overline{x}+yz$ is the minimal SOP.

pitfalls: Multiplying out all five clauses blindly — the distributive law gives the answer in two lines.
cse-1997-b-71-a.verification: Truth check: $w=1,x=0,y=0,z=0$ — clause $(\overline{w}+y)=0$ so $f=0$; formula gives $0+0=0$. ✓

cse-1997-b-71-b.approach: A stuck-at-0 output is wrong exactly where f should be 1, so count the minterms of f = w′x′ + yz by inclusion–exclusion.

steps.title: When is the output wrong?
steps.body: Output stuck at 0 ⇒ correct whenever $f=0$, wrong whenever $f=1$. Count the 1s of $f=\overline{w}\,\overline{x}+yz$ (from (a)).

steps.title: Count
steps.body:
$|\overline{w}\,\overline{x}|=2^2=4$, $|yz|=2^2=4$, overlap $\overline{w}\,\overline{x}yz$: $1$.

$4+4-1=7$ input combinations.

pitfalls: Adding 4 + 4 = 8 and double counting w′x′yz.
cse-1997-b-71-b.verification: K-map 1-cells: m0, m1, m2, m3, m7, m11, m15 — seven cells.

animation.title: Cells where f = 1 (wrong when stuck at 0)

cse-1997-b-72-a.approach: Convert to binary, normalise to 0.1xxxx × 2^e, keep 5 magnitude bits (truncating the rest) and write the exponent in 4-bit sign-magnitude.
cse-1997-b-72-a.given:
| Field | Bits | Form |
|---|---|---|
| $f$ (mantissa) | 6 = sign + 5 | sign-magnitude fraction $0.b_1\dots b_5$ |
| $e$ (exponent) | 4 = sign + 3 | sign-magnitude integer |
pitfalls: Using an unnormalised mantissa (e.g. 0.01101 × 2^7) and losing a significant bit.
Rounding instead of truncating — the question's error part (c) assumes the bits are simply dropped.

cse-1997-b-72-b.approach: Standard FP addition: equalise exponents by shifting the smaller operand's mantissa right, add mantissas, then normalise.
cse-1997-b-72-b.given:
| Field | Bits | Form |
|---|---|---|
| $f$ (mantissa) | 6 = sign + 5 | sign-magnitude fraction $0.b_1\dots b_5$ |
| $e$ (exponent) | 4 = sign + 3 | sign-magnitude integer |

steps.title: Compare exponents
steps.body: $e_A=6$, $e_B=4$; difference $6-4=2$, so shift B's mantissa right by 2.

steps.title: Align B
steps.body: $0.10011\times2^4\to0.0010011\times2^6\to0.00100\times2^6$ (5 bits kept; the shifted-out $11$ is lost).

pitfalls: Shifting the larger operand left instead of the smaller one right.
cse-1997-b-72-b.verification: 54 + 8 = 62, where 8 is the aligned value 0.001 × 2^6 of B.

cse-1997-b-72-c.approach: Compare the computed sum 62 with the true sum 54.75 + 9.75 = 64.5.
pitfalls: Dividing by the computed value 62 (gives 4.0%) — relative error uses the true value.

cse-1997-b-73.approach: request_R either grants R immediately or records the request. release_R, inside the mutex, hands R directly to the highest-priority recorded requester (V on its semaphore) and keeps busy = true; only if nobody waits does it set busy = false.

steps.title: What release_R must do
steps.body: Waiting processes are blocked on $P(\text{proceed}[p])$ with $R\_requested[p]=\text{true}$. On release, scan priorities $3,2,1$; wake the first requester and clear its flag. The resource passes directly, so **busy stays true**. If no flag is set, set busy := false.

steps.title: Pseudo code
Why it is correct
steps.body: All tests of busy and the flags are inside $P(\text{mutex})\dots V(\text{mutex})$, so a request cannot slip in between the scan and the update. Because busy is never set false while someone is waiting, a newly arriving low-priority process cannot grab R ahead of a waiter, and each waiter is woken in priority order. Priorities are unique, so at most one process waits on each $\text{proceed}[p]$.

answer.value: procedure release_R(priority); P(mutex); if R_requested[3] then begin R_requested[3] := false; V(proceed[3]) end else if R_requested[2] then begin R_requested[2] := false; V(proceed[2]) end else if R_requested[1] then begin R_requested[1] := false; V(proceed[1]) end else busy := false; V(mutex);

pitfalls: Setting busy := false before waking a waiter — a new request could then take R out of priority order.
Forgetting to reset R_requested[p], which would hand R to the same process twice.
Doing the scan outside the mutex (race with request_R).
cse-1997-b-73.verification: Traced: P1 holds R, P2 and P3 request (flags set, both blocked). On P1 release, P3 is woken and busy stays true; on P3 release P2 is woken; on P2 release no flag is set, so busy := false.

cse-1997-b-74-a.approach: Without buffering nothing overlaps: each record costs access + transfer + processing in sequence.
cse-1997-b-74-a.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Records | 1000 × 3200 B |
| Access time | 10 ms |
| Transfer of one record | $3200/(800\times10^3)$ s $=4$ ms |
| CPU per record | 3 ms |

steps.title: Time per record
steps.body: Read: $10+4=14$ ms; process: $3$ ms; total $14+3=17$ ms.

steps.title: All 1000 records
steps.body: $1000\times17\text{ ms}=17000\text{ ms}=17$ s.

cse-1997-b-74-a.verification: Gantt of the first two records: read 0–14, CPU 14–17, read 17–31, CPU 31–34 — 17 ms per record.
pitfalls: Converting the transfer rate wrongly: 3200 B at 800 000 B/s is 4 ms, not 0.4 ms.
Overlapping I/O with processing — without a buffer the program reads, then processes, strictly in sequence.

cse-1997-b-74-b.approach: With one read-ahead buffer, reading record i+1 overlaps processing record i. Reading (14 ms) is slower than processing (3 ms), so the disk is the bottleneck: 1000 reads back to back plus the processing of the last record.
cse-1997-b-74-b.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Records | 1000 × 3200 B |
| Access time | 10 ms |
| Transfer of one record | $3200/(800\times10^3)$ s $=4$ ms |
| CPU per record | 3 ms |

steps.title: Overlap pattern
steps.body: When R1 arrives at 14 ms it is moved to P's variable (negligible time) and the read of R2 starts at once, while the CPU processes R1 (14–17 ms). The CPU then idles until R2 arrives at 28 ms.

steps.title: Total
steps.body:
Disk busy continuously: $1000\times14=14000$ ms. The last record is processed after its read: $+3$ ms.

$$14000+3=14003\text{ ms}=14.003\text{ s}\approx14\text{ s}$$

pitfalls: Adding CPU time for every record (17 s) — processing hides behind the next read.
cse-1997-b-74-b.verification: Gantt: reads end at 14, 28, 42 ms …; record k is processed in [14k, 14k+3]; last ends at 14000 + 3.

cse-1997-b-74-c.approach: Blocking factor 2 halves the number of accesses: 500 block reads of 10 + 8 = 18 ms each, overlapped with processing of the previous block (6 ms), plus processing of the last block.
cse-1997-b-74-c.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Records | 1000 × 3200 B |
| Access time | 10 ms |
| Transfer of one record | $3200/(800\times10^3)$ s $=4$ ms |
| CPU per record | 3 ms |

steps.title: One block
steps.body: Block = 2 records = 6400 B. Read: $10+\dfrac{6400}{800\times10^3}\text{ s}=10+8=18$ ms. Processing a block: $2\times3=6$ ms $<18$ ms, so the disk is the bottleneck.

steps.title: Total
steps.body:
$1000/2=500$ blocks: $500\times18=9000$ ms, plus processing of the last block $6$ ms.

$$9000+6=9006\text{ ms}=9.006\text{ s}\approx9\text{ s}$$

pitfalls: Paying the 10 ms access per record instead of per block.
Adding only 3 ms at the end — the whole last block (2 records) is processed after the final read.
cse-1997-b-74-c.verification: Reads end at 18, 36, 54 … 9000 ms; the last block is processed 9000–9006 ms.

cse-1997-b-75-a.approach: This is the wound–wait scheme. Show that every wait-for edge goes from a younger process (larger TS) to an older one (smaller TS); timestamps are a strict order, so the wait-for graph can never contain a cycle.

steps.title: Direction of every wait
steps.body: A process P waits only in rule (ii), i.e. when the holder Q has $TS(Q)<TS(P)$. In rule (iii) an older requester never waits — it takes the resource. When a holder releases, the resource goes to the waiter with the smallest TS, so every remaining waiter is younger than the new holder and keeps waiting for an **older** process.

steps.title: No cycle
steps.body: So every edge $P\to Q$ of the wait-for graph satisfies $TS(P)>TS(Q)$. A cycle $P_1\to P_2\to\dots\to P_1$ would need $TS(P_1)>TS(P_2)>\dots>TS(P_1)$ — impossible since timestamps are unique and totally ordered. Hence **deadlock can never arise**.

pitfalls: Confusing with wait–die: here the older process preempts (wounds) the younger holder.
cse-1997-b-75-a.verification: Example: P(TS 1) holds R1, Q(TS 2) holds R2. Q requests R1 → waits (older holder). P requests R2 → Q is restarted, P gets R2. No cycle forms.

cse-1997-b-75-b.approach: A restarted process keeps its timestamp, and new processes get larger timestamps. So a process only ever has finitely many older processes, and once it is the oldest it can never wait or be restarted.

steps.title: The oldest process always finishes
steps.body: Let P have the smallest timestamp in the system. It never waits (no holder is older) and is never restarted (only an older requester can restart it). Since there is no deadlock (part a), it obtains every resource it requests and finishes in finite time.

steps.title: Every process becomes the oldest
steps.body: Timestamps are kept on restart and later arrivals get larger timestamps, so the set of processes older than P is finite and never grows. Each of them finishes in finite time (by induction on timestamp order), after which P is the oldest and finishes too. Hence **no process starves**.

pitfalls: Assuming a restarted process gets a fresh (larger) timestamp — then it could be wounded forever; keeping the old timestamp is exactly what prevents starvation.
cse-1997-b-75-b.verification: A process can be restarted only by strictly older processes, of which there are finitely many, so it can be restarted only finitely often.

cse-1997-b-76-a.approach: Translate SQL directly: FROM → Cartesian product, WHERE → selection, SELECT → projection.

steps.title: Map each clause
steps.body: FROM EMP, INVOLVED $\to EMP\times INVOLVED$; WHERE $\to\sigma_{EMP.eno=INVOLVED.eno\,\wedge\,INVOLVED.pno=3}$; SELECT eno $\to\pi_{eno}$.

steps.title: Expression
steps.body:
$$\pi_{eno}\big(\sigma_{EMP.eno=INVOLVED.eno\ \wedge\ INVOLVED.pno=3}(EMP\times INVOLVED)\big)$$
(Equivalently $\pi_{eno}(\sigma_{pno=3}(INVOLVED))$, since every eno in INVOLVED is also in EMP.)

pitfalls: Using natural join ⋈ — it is not in the allowed operator set {σ, π, ×, ∪, −}.
cse-1997-b-76-a.verification: Each row of the product that survives the selection pairs an employee with one of his rows having pno = 3; projecting eno gives exactly the SQL result.

cse-1997-b-76-b-i.approach: Recognise the standard division pattern: (all employees × all projects) − actual pairs gives the missing pairs; employees with a missing pair are removed.

steps.title: Inner part
steps.body: $\pi_{eno}(INVOLVED)\times\pi_{pno}(PROJ)$ = every (employee, project) combination. Subtracting INVOLVED leaves the pairs where the employee is **not** in that project. $\pi_{eno}$ of that = employees missing at least one project.

steps.title: Outer difference
steps.body: $\pi_{eno}(INVOLVED)$ minus those = employees involved in **every** project, i.e. $INVOLVED\div\pi_{pno}(PROJ)$.

answer.value: Employees (eno) who are involved in every project

pitfalls: Reading it as "employees not in any project" — the subtraction removes only those who miss some project.
cse-1997-b-76-b-i.verification: Example: projects {1, 2}; INVOLVED = {(e1,1),(e1,2),(e2,1)}. Missing pairs {(e2,2)} → result {e1}, the only employee in all projects.

cse-1997-b-76-b-ii.approach: Read the second term as $\pi_{E.age}(\sigma_{E.age<EMP.age}(\rho_E(EMP)\times EMP))$: the ages that are smaller than some other age. Subtracting them from all ages leaves the largest age.

steps.title: Interpret the printed expression
steps.body: The subscript $E.age<EMP.age$ is a selection condition on $\rho_E(EMP)\times EMP$ (the paper merges $\sigma$ into $\pi$). The pairs kept are those where the copy's age is less than some employee's age; the projected ages are therefore the **non-maximum** ages.

steps.title: Difference
steps.body: $\pi_{age}(EMP)$ − (ages that are less than some other age) = ages not less than any age = the **maximum age**, i.e. the age of the oldest employee(s).

answer.value: The maximum age among employees (age of the oldest employee)

pitfalls: Projecting EMP.age instead of E.age would remove the non-minimum ages and give the minimum — the projected attribute is E.age.
cse-1997-b-76-b-ii.verification: Ages {25, 30, 40}: ages smaller than some other = {25, 30}; difference = {40}, the maximum.
